To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the order of recalls of premises and conclusions in a set inclusion task is not random, and (2) reaction times to the conclusion are longer than reaction times to the premises, which indicates that the premises are encoded in a propositional representation, and the conclusion in an integrated representation.
the order of recall of premises is not a reliable indicator of the order of encoding and that the order of encoding of premises is not necessarily the order of encoding inferences.
the mental models approach does not account for transitive inference performance.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the nature and the construction of representations of relations in memory.
how the human mind processes information.
the question of the representation of the relations between objects in the world and the way they are encoded in the mind.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
mental models and propositional representations can be used to represent the same relations, but that the choice of representation is dependent on the relation to be processed.
, in the case of the set inclusion relation, the construction of an adequate representation requires that the propositional representation of each sentence be coordinated in a specific manner.
the construction of a mental model is a necessary but not a sufficient condition for the production of inferences.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the construction of a mental model of the text is not a sufficient condition for solving the transitive inference task.
the encoding of a set inclusion relation does not result in a mental model.
the representation of a set inclusion relation involves a propositional representation that is not necessarily organized as a mental model.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we need to take into account the nature of the relations that are represented.

the mental models and the propositional theories of reasoning are both correct in their own way, but the former is correct for linear ordering relations, while the latter is correct for set relations.
the mental models approach to deductive reasoning is not a general theory of human reasoning.
